chapters.title: From dangerous elements to table salt

lines.cap: Here are two dangerous elements: a soft metal that can explode in water, and a poisonous green gas once used as a weapon in war.
They're **sodium** and **chlorine**. Join them together, and they make **table salt**, which you sprinkle on your chips.
How? It all comes down to **atoms**, and whether they're **joined** together or just **mixed**.
Let's meet **elements**, **compounds** and **mixtures**, then learn how chemists pull mixtures apart.
Everything around you, from the air to your phone, is made of tiny particles called **atoms**, too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.
An **element** is a substance made of only **one type of atom**. Every atom in a bar of pure gold is a gold atom.
With only one kind of atom, an element **can't be broken down** into anything simpler by a chemical reaction.
There are about **118** elements, all listed in the **periodic table**: oxygen, iron, gold, carbon, hydrogen and the rest.
Each element has a **chemical symbol** of one or two letters. Carbon is **C**, oxygen is **O**, and magnesium is **Mg**.
The rules are strict: the **first letter is always a capital**, and any **second letter is always lower case**.
Think **Big then small**. Sodium is **Na**: a big N, followed by a small a.
It really matters. **Co**, with a small o, is the metal **cobalt**. But **CO**, with two capitals, is **carbon monoxide**, a compound of carbon and oxygen.
When atoms of **two or more different elements** are **chemically bonded** together, they make a **compound**.
The atoms are joined in a **fixed ratio**, which never changes for that compound.
**Water** is always two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Its **formula** is **H₂O**.
**Carbon dioxide** is one carbon and two oxygens: **CO₂**. Table salt, **sodium chloride**, is **NaCl**: one sodium for every chlorine.
The small numbers written low are **subscripts**. Each one counts the atom just before it, and no number means one.
Leave one out, and you've written something else: **HO** isn't water, and **CO** isn't carbon dioxide.
Now the most surprising idea: a compound has **completely different properties** from the elements in it.
Hydrogen is an explosive gas, and oxygen helps things burn. Yet bonded together as **water**, they put fires out.
Remember sodium and chlorine? A dangerous metal and a poisonous gas, bonded together, make **harmless table salt**.
So the properties of a substance depend not just on its atoms, but on **how they're joined**.
Making or breaking a compound takes a **chemical reaction**, so it's hard to split one back into its elements.
A **molecule** is a particle made of **two or more atoms joined together** by chemical bonds.
Some molecules contain only **one element**. Oxygen gas is made of **O₂** molecules: two oxygen atoms, joined. Hydrogen is **H₂**, and nitrogen is **N₂**.
They're still **elements**, because every atom is the same type.
Other molecules contain different elements. **Water** and **carbon dioxide** are molecules of **compounds**.
Scientists draw **particle pictures** to show the difference. Each circle is an atom. Its **colour** shows its type, and if atoms are drawn **joined**, they're bonded.
To read one, ask two questions. Are the atoms the **same or different**? And are they **joined**, or just **mixed**?
All the atoms the same colour, alone or in identical molecules? That's an **element**.
Different atoms **joined** in identical groups? That's a **compound**.
Different particles, **not joined** to each other, just jumbled together? That's a **mixture**.
Remember: **Same, Bonded, Free**. Element: same atoms. Compound: different atoms, bonded. Mixture: particles free.
One trap: identical atoms joined in pairs are bonded, but they're still an **element**. A compound needs **different** elements.
A **mixture** is two or more substances **mixed together**, but **not chemically bonded**.
Because nothing is bonded, each substance **keeps its own properties**.
You can mix them in **any ratio**, a little or a lot. A compound's ratio is always fixed.
And you can usually **separate** them again by **physical methods**, with no chemical reaction needed.
**Air** is a mixture of gases: about **78% nitrogen** and **21% oxygen**, plus a little argon and carbon dioxide.
**Sea water** is a mixture too: water with salt and other substances dissolved in it.
**Alloys** are mixtures of metals, or of a metal and carbon. **Brass** is copper and zinc; **steel** is iron and carbon.
An alloy looks like one shiny metal, but it's a **mixture**: its metals aren't bonded in a fixed ratio, and the recipe can vary.
Even gold jewellery is usually an alloy. Pure gold is so soft that other metals are added to make it tough enough to wear.
So a compound isn't just a very well-mixed mixture. A compound is **bonded**, in a **fixed ratio**, and takes a **chemical reaction** to make or break.
A mixture is **not bonded**, can be in **any ratio**, and comes apart by **physical methods**.
In everyday life, '**pure** orange juice' just means nothing has been added. In chemistry, pure means something much stricter.
A **pure substance** is a **single element or a single compound**, with nothing else mixed in. Pure water is **only** H₂O.
Anything with other substances mixed in is **impure**. It's really a mixture.
So how can you tell? Measure its **melting point**, or its **boiling point**.
A pure substance melts and boils at **one exact, sharp temperature**. Pure ice melts at exactly **0 °C**, and pure water boils at **100 °C**.
But an impurity **lowers the melting point** and **raises the boiling point**, spreading each one over a **range** of temperatures.
That's why we **grit icy roads**. The salt lowers the melting point of the ice, so it melts even below **0 °C**.
Chemists check their products this way. A medicine that melts **sharply**, at just the right temperature, is very likely pure.
But is anything ever **100% pure**? Not quite. There are always tiny traces of something else, so 'pure enough' depends on the job.
Stir sugar into tea and it seems to vanish. It has **dissolved**, making a mixture called a **solution**.
The **solute** is what dissolves, like the sugar. The **solvent** is the liquid it's **in**, like the water. Together they make the **solution**.
A substance that dissolves, like salt, is **soluble**. One that doesn't, like sand, is **insoluble**.
Keep adding sugar, and eventually no more will dissolve at that temperature: the solution is **saturated**.
The most solute that can dissolve in a fixed amount of solvent is its **solubility**. It usually **rises with temperature**: hot tea dissolves more sugar than cold.
**Concentration** tells you how much solute is dissolved in a given volume. A **dilute** solution has **few** solute particles; a **concentrated** one has **many**.
Think of squash. Add more squash to make it more **concentrated**, or more water to make it more **dilute**.
And a dissolved solute is **not destroyed**. Its particles are still there, just spread out between the water particles.
Dissolve **10 g** of salt in **100 g** of water, and the solution weighs **110 g**. Nothing is lost, and **evaporating** the water gets the salt back.
A mixture isn't bonded, so **physical methods** can separate it. The trick is choosing the right one.
**Filtration** separates an **insoluble solid** from a **liquid**, like sand from water.
Pour the mixture through **filter paper** in a funnel. The solid bits are too big to fit through the paper's tiny holes.
The liquid that passes through is the **filtrate**. The solid left on the paper is the **residue**.
But you **can't filter salt water**. The salt is dissolved, and its tiny particles slip straight through the paper.
To get a dissolved solid back, heat the solution in an **evaporating basin**. The water **evaporates**, and the solid is left behind.
For purer, better-shaped crystals, use **crystallisation**. First, gently heat the solution to evaporate **some** of the water, until it's **saturated**.
Then stop heating, and leave it to **cool slowly**. Neat **crystals** grow as the solute comes out of the solution.
Finally, **filter** off the crystals and **dry** them, by patting them with filter paper or leaving them somewhere warm.
So filtration traps an **undissolved** solid, while evaporation and crystallisation recover a **dissolved** one.
Try it at home: stir salty sand into warm water, filter out the sand, and leave the clear liquid on a dark plate. Salt crystals appear in a day or two.
What if you want the **water** back, not the salt? Use **simple distillation**.
Heat the salt water. The water **boils** into vapour, but the salt, with a far higher boiling point, stays behind.
The vapour passes into a **condenser**, where it **cools** and **condenses** back into liquid. Pure water drips into a clean beaker.
So remember: **evaporation keeps the solid**, but **distillation keeps the liquid**.
**Fractional distillation** separates a mixture of **liquids** with **different boiling points**, using a tall **fractionating column**.
The liquid with the **lowest boiling point** comes off first, at the top of the column.
That's how **crude oil** is split into petrol, diesel and jet fuel, and how liquid air is split into nitrogen and oxygen.
**Chromatography** separates **coloured substances**, like the dyes in an ink.
Put a spot of ink near the bottom of special paper, and stand it in a **solvent**, with the spot just above the liquid.
As the solvent soaks upwards, each dye travels a **different distance**, depending on how soluble it is and how much it sticks to the paper.
It can **identify** substances too. Run known dyes beside the unknown: if two spots end up **level**, they're very likely the **same substance**.
That's how **forensic scientists** can match the ink on a note to a particular pen.
Try it with a felt-tip pen, a strip of kitchen paper and a little water. One black ink can split into several colours!
Two more methods complete your toolkit.
Some liquids, like **oil and water**, don't mix. These **immiscible** liquids settle into two **layers**, with the less dense oil on top.
Pour them into a **separating funnel**: a glass funnel with a **tap** at the bottom.
Open the tap, and the **lower layer**, the water, drains out first. Close it just as the boundary reaches the tap, and the oil stays behind.
**Magnetic separation** is for mixtures where one solid is **magnetic**, like **iron filings** mixed with sand or sulfur.
Hold a **magnet** over the mixture. It pulls out the iron, and leaves the rest behind.
But it only works for magnetic metals, such as **iron**, **steel**, **nickel** and **cobalt**.
So, to choose a method, ask: are the substances solids, liquids or dissolved? Do they mix? Is anything magnetic?
And remember **FECD**: **Filter** an insoluble solid, **Evaporate** or **Crystallise** a dissolved one, and **Distil** to get the liquid back.
Now a puzzle: sand, iron filings and salt, all jumbled together. How would you get all three back?
Use a **magnet** for the iron. Then add water to dissolve the salt, **filter** out the sand, and **crystallise** the salt.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Same, Bonded, Free**: an element has the same atoms; a compound has different atoms, bonded; a mixture's particles are free.
**Big then small**: a capital first letter, and a lower-case second letter, as in **Na** and **Mg**.
The **solute** is what dissolves; the **solvent** is the liquid it's **in**.
**FECD**: Filter, Evaporate, Crystallise, Distil.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: two capitals means a compound. Cobalt is **Co**, but **CO** is carbon monoxide.
Two: you **can't filter** salt out of salt water. Evaporate it, or distil it.
Three: **evaporation** keeps the solid; **distillation** keeps the liquid.
Four: impurities **lower** the melting point, and spread it over a range.
Five: a dissolved solute isn't destroyed. It's still there, and its mass is **conserved**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
What's the chemical formula for water?
**H₂O**: two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.
Air: is it an element, a compound or a mixture?
A **mixture**. Its gases are mixed, but not bonded.
How does an impurity change a substance's melting point?
It **lowers** it, and spreads it over a **range**.
Which method separates the different dyes in an ink?
**Chromatography.**
True or false: when sugar dissolves in water, it's destroyed.
**False.** Its particles spread out among the water particles, and the mass stays the same.
Brilliant work. Now try the Elements, Compounds and Mixtures quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
